introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá grants that “the saints and mystics had real experiences” and gives one test: “the proof of the experience was its fruit.” The guide then moves through the language of the mystical path as the Báb, Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá use it: annihilation and bewilderment, veils and stations, Sinai and the burning tree, separation and longing, the reed-flute and the nightingale, fragrance, and above all a sealed wine now unsealed. Much of that language is older than the readings and they quote it; so Rúmí’s reed, Ḥalláj’s cry, Sa‘dí’s moth and the Qur’án’s Light Verse and sealed wine are set beside them. The Song of Solomon and the psalms speak the same tongue of longing, as do Plato’s ladder of beauty, Julian’s hazel nut, Blake’s grain of sand and Herbert’s feast. The sceptics are heard too: Hobbes on voices, Theseus on lovers and madmen, Nietzsche on fidelity to the earth, Descartes on clarity, Hillel on leaving the community, and FitzGerald’s Khayyám, whose wine may be only wine.
questions: “The proof of the experience was its fruit.” Hobbes says a man who reports that God spoke to him has told us only that he dreamed it. What fruits would count as an answer, and which of the guide’s last readings describe them?
The readings say the pen cannot carry the mystery, and Wittgenstein says that whereof one cannot speak one must be silent. Why, then, so much speech in images of wine, fragrance and birds?
None ascends “save through love of Thy loved ones,” and John’s letter says God is love; yet one reading speaks of a plane where “love is a veil.” How do you read these together?

Ḥalláj’s “I am He whom I love” is defended in the readings by Shabistarí’s couplet, and Isaiah’s God gives his glory to no other. What distinguishes self-effacement from self-exaltation when their words are the same?
How does a reader tell the wine of the Qur’án, Bahá’u’lláh and Herbert from the wine of FitzGerald’s Khayyám, and does it matter that the image is the same?
The mystic prays alone on the mountain, and Hillel says not to separate from the community. Where do the guide’s readings bring the solitary traveller back?

outside.why: “The proof of the experience was its fruit.” Jesus gives the same test for anyone who claims to speak for God: ye shall know them by their fruits.

“Most assuredly the saints and mystics had real experiences.” William James, surveying them as a psychologist in 1902, found that the creeds cancel one another but that there is a certain uniform deliverance in which religions all appear to meet.
Annihilation means that one “should wholly annihilate himself in God.” Paul’s sentence for it: I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.

The mystic is to “transcend the pleasures and promptings of the mortal world.” Nietzsche’s Zarathustra begs for the opposite loyalty: remain true to the earth, and believe not those who speak unto you of superearthly hopes. What does each think the other despises?
None rises into that atmosphere “save through love of Thy loved ones.” The First Letter of John: he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?

Love of God’s friends is “identical with Thy love.” Leigh Hunt’s Abou, not found among those who love the Lord, asks to be written as one that loves his fellow men, and next night his name leads all the rest.
“Every invisible must have a visible manifestation, and every word must possess a meaning.” John’s prologue: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory.

The mystics are charged with contenting themselves with “an imaginary Invisible One.” The author of The Cloud of Unknowing would agree that thought cannot reach God and says what can: by love may he be gotten and holden. Is that the contentment the reading rejects?

“What capacity have pen and paper to become intimate with inner mysteries?” The elder who wrote the Third Letter of John breaks off for the same reason: I will not with ink and pen write unto thee; we shall speak face to face.

The pen cannot be privy to the mystery. Wittgenstein ends his book with the rule that seems to follow: whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent. The readings go on speaking, in images. Is that disobedience to the rule or another kind of speech?
“Increase my bewilderment in Thee!” The psalmist before God’s knowledge of him: such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.

Bewilderment is called “beloved.” Descartes made it his first rule never to accept anything as true that he did not clearly know to be such. Is there a bewilderment that knowledge should cure and another that it should reach?
“We have worlds within this world”; the sun can be shown in an atom. Julian of Norwich was shown a little thing the size of a hazel nut in the palm of her hand, and was told: it is all that is made.

“Love is a veil betwixt the lover and the beloved,” and in this plane love “becometh but an obstructing veil.” The First Letter of John puts nothing beyond love: he that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love. What could the reading mean by a station where love falls away?

Some receive “according to a known measure,” others “without account.” In Jesus’s parable those hired at the eleventh hour are paid as those who bore the heat of the day, and the householder asks: is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own?

The customs of the spiritual realms are “beyond all bounds and measures.” Paul, quoting Isaiah: eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared.

From the Primal Point “diverse forms became manifest.” Plotinus on how the many come from the One: seeking nothing, possessing nothing, lacking nothing, it has overflowed, and its exuberance has produced the new.

The hidden crafts in all things are perfected “that the tongues of all things might proclaim His power.” Hopkins: the world is charged with the grandeur of God; it will flame out, like shining from shook foil.

The Báb describes a descent of “the water of divine manifestation” through its stations. Lao Tzu takes water for the pattern of the highest excellence because it benefits all things and settles in the low place.
Less than a needle’s eye of the light is shown upon the Mount. The Qur’án tells what a mountain did when its Lord revealed His glory to it, and what became of Moses.
“We know that which no one knoweth besides Us.” Deuteronomy divides what is known: the secret things belong unto the Lord our God, but those things which are revealed belong unto us.
“Do you not reflect upon the creation of the heavens and your own selves?” The Qur’án’s verse behind the question: and also in yourselves; can ye then not see?
“The baptism of water, of spirit and of fire.” John the Baptist names all three at the Jordan: I baptize you with water; he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire.
Shabistarí’s couplet defends the cry “I am the Truth,” for which al-Ḥalláj was put to death in 922. These are Ḥalláj’s own lines: I am He whom I love, and He whom I love is I.

If a bush may say it, why not a blessed person? Isaiah’s God speaks in the first person and shares the word with no one: I am the Lord; my glory will I not give to another. Where is the line between the mystic’s cry and the claim this verse forbids?

“A hundred thousand … each one a Moses, cry, ‘O Lord! Allow my gaze to fall upon Thy Beauty!’” The answer Moses himself received in Exodus: thou shalt see my back parts, but my face shall not be seen.
“That call which the Son of ‘Imrán heard.” The Qur’án’s telling: he was called from the right side of the valley, from the tree: O Moses! Lo! I, even I, am Allah, the Lord of the Worlds.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes a phrase of the Light Verse: “its oil would almost glow though no fire touched it.” Here is the verse, with its niche, lamp, glass and blessed tree.

“Through the removal of the veil this bounty is attained - there is no intermediary.” The First Letter to Timothy makes a mediator the centre of faith: one God, and one mediator between God and men. How do the readings elsewhere hold both?
The heart “is a mirror reflecting the beauty of the free.” Zhuangzi on the perfected person: he employs his mind as a mirror; it grasps nothing, it refuses nothing.
The sign of His dominion “manifest in a speck of dust” cannot be confined. Blake: to see a world in a grain of sand, and a heaven in a wild flower.
The Sun may be veiled by clouds while its light grows stronger. John: the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
“Tear asunder the veil and see the realities of things with the eye of God.” Blake: if the doors of perception were cleansed every thing would appear to man as it is, infinite.
“Until they cross over the gulf of names they shall not enter the Most Great Ocean.” The Chāndogya Upaniṣad: the rivers, when they are in the sea, do not know, I am this or that river.
“All are in a strange slumber.” The early hymn quoted in Ephesians: awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead.

The Countenances are stripped of “the veils of otherness” and of blind imagination. Shelley says of great poetry that veil after veil may be undrawn and the inmost naked beauty of the meaning never exposed. Is there a last veil?

Station after station, and then “the heaven of wonderment.” Diotima’s ladder in the Symposium ends the same way: he who has learned to see the beautiful in due order will suddenly perceive a nature of wondrous beauty.
They have “chosen solitude with the Beloved.” The Song of Solomon’s shortest verse: my beloved is mine, and I am his.
“Nor can the ocean cool the heat of longing.” The Song of Solomon: many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
Seas surge in their hearts, “and yet they breathe not a word thereof.” Lao Tzu: he who knows does not speak; he who speaks does not know.
“No trace thereof is to be seen.” Colossians on the believer’s real life: ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.
A station “recorded … in hidden script.” The promise to the church at Pergamos: a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.

The traveller is to turn away from the questioner, having reached “a city whose gates God hath shut against the likes of thee.” Jesus sends his secrets the other way: what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops. When is silence about the journey reverence, and when is it pride?
“I journeyed from Thee unto Thee, and by Thee I migrated toward Thee.” Paul’s doxology has the three prepositions: of him, and through him, and to him, are all things.
He “sat before Thee and dwelt in Thy presence.” The psalmist’s single wish: to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the Lord.
“With torn collar, naked, mad and intoxicated.” The bystanders at Pentecost reached for the same explanation: these men are full of new wine.
“Until the candle burns it gives no light.” Sa‘dí’s moth is the other half of the image: it burnt, lost its life, and found no voice.
“How long, O my God, shall I melt in the fire of separation?” The psalm begins with the same two words: how long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? for ever?
“Separation from Thee hath destroyed me, and nearness to Thee is my hope.” Augustine: our heart is restless, until it repose in thee.
Lovers “wandering, aimlessly and perplexedly, in the wilderness of longing.” The Song of Solomon: by night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.
The nightingale of the divine rose garden “harmonizes with spiritual melodies.” Keats, listening in a Hampstead garden: thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!

Bahá’u’lláh quotes Rúmí’s verse of the shaykh who went about the city with a lamp, wanting human company. Rúmí took the figure from the story of Diogenes: he lit a lamp in broad daylight and said, I am looking for a man.
“I am the reed-flute, Thou the Player!” Rúmí’s Masnaví opens with that flute: listen to the reed, how it tells a tale, complaining of separations.

“Known for my madness … though ere this I was foremost among the wise.” Theseus has a cool word for all such: the lunatic, the lover and the poet are of imagination all compact. What can the lover say to Theseus?
Melodies “from the eternal lute and harp.” Keats: heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard are sweeter; pipe to the spirit ditties of no tone.
A friend’s “musk-laden pen.” Proverbs has the same pairing: ointment and perfume rejoice the heart; so doth the sweetness of a man’s friend by hearty counsel.
A letter’s journey is compared to the ascent on Buráq. The verse of the Night Journey: glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place.
A fragrance by which “the atmosphere of sacred divine existence” is perfumed. Paul: God maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place; we are unto God a sweet savour.
A singer who “was not a professional artist but a mystic worshipper,” whose singing “was not mechanical.” Shelley’s skylark pours its full heart in profuse strains of unpremeditated art.
Music by which listeners are drawn “to the colorless realm.” Shelley: life, like a dome of many-coloured glass, stains the white radiance of Eternity.
Sing “until … the outpouring of the Holy Spirit manifests.” Joel’s promise: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions.
“The Maid of beauty shone forth even as the dawning sun.” The Song of Solomon: who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun?
A heavenly Maiden stands for what draws the soul. The closing chorus of Faust speaks of all things transitory as symbols, and ends with the Eternal-Feminine that draws us on.
“Through Him were the heavens raised up.” John: all things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.
A Book by which “God distinguished between the believers and the ungodly.” Hebrews: the word of God is sharper than any twoedged sword, a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
“Blessed be they who behold!” Jesus to his disciples: blessed are your eyes, for they see; many prophets have desired to see those things which ye see.
Tidings at the ear, and “I trembled.” Eliphaz in Job: a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up; there was silence, and I heard a voice.

A voice stirs at the ear and all creation trembles with the hearer. Hobbes on any such report: to say God hath spoken to him in a dream is no more than to say he dreamed that God spake to him. What, on the first reading’s own test, would answer Hobbes?
“The Eternal Dove on the everlasting branch.” At the Jordan the Spirit of God is seen descending like a dove.
“The nightingales of mystic knowledge are warbling upon the branches.” The Song of Solomon: the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land.
“While the gates of reunion are open, hasten!” Isaiah: seek ye the Lord while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near.
“While the flower is at market, lament.” Herrick uses the same flower for another urgency: gather ye rosebuds while ye may, old Time is still a-flying. What separates the two kinds of haste?

Detach from all that has been seen and heard, then look “with the eye and ear of truth and fairness.” Bacon on why that is hard: the human understanding is no dry light, but receives an infusion from the will and affections.
“The Mystery and the Mystery of the Mystery.” The early Christian hymn in First Timothy begins: without controversy great is the mystery of godliness.

The Sealed Wine, “though ever in people’s hands, remained sealed.” Isaiah: the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed; one cannot read it for it is sealed, another for he is not learned.
“The seal of the Choice Wine [was] broken.” John weeps because no man is found worthy to open the book and to loose its seven seals, until one is found.
“The sealed flask hath been unsealed.” The image is the Qur’án’s, among the rewards of the righteous: they are given to drink of a pure wine, sealed.
“Take thou the chalice of salvation.” The psalmist: I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord.
Crimson cups are passed round to the people of the Kingdom. Paul on the cup Christians share: the cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?

He gives His servants to drink. Jesus at the supper looks ahead to another cup: I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.
A wine that “at every moment increases one’s love for Him.” The Song of Solomon measures the two against each other: thy love is better than wine.

In this wine “are concealed effects and hidden wisdoms.” FitzGerald’s Khayyám uses the same cup and tavern and seems to mean the vintage: a jug of wine, a loaf of bread, and thou. How does a reader of Persian poetry know which wine is meant?
“Thou hast anointed thine eyes with that sacred earth.” The counsel to the church at Laodicea: anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.
Wine from the Cup-Bearer and bread “from the banquet table of God.” The shepherd psalm: thou preparest a table before me; my cup runneth over.
“From the sweet-scented streams of Thine eternity give me to drink.” A psalm: thou shalt make them drink of the river of thy pleasures.
“Partake of the heavenly feast from the table of divine bounty.” The Song of Solomon: he brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.
“You have found repose in the shade of the Divine Lote-Tree.” The Song: I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.
“The cup mingled with camphor is passing round.” The phrase is from the Qur’án’s chapter on Man: the righteous shall drink of a cup whereof the mixture is of Káfúr.
The friends receive their share of “mystic wine.” George Herbert’s guest hangs back, guilty of dust and sin, until Love says: you must sit down and taste my meat. So I did sit and eat.
“Intoxicated with the wine of ‘Am I not your Lord?’” The Qur’án’s scene of the first covenant, when the seed of Adam answered: Yea, verily.

Cups move “as if they were drawn by the magnet of our Lord’s” love. Socrates explains inspiration to a reciter by the same stone: the magnet attracts iron rings and gives them the power to attract others, so that a chain hangs from it.
“Hearken to the murmuring of the waters of inner meanings.” The psalmist: deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts.
“At times the fragrance of the garment is diffused from it.” The garment is Joseph’s shirt, whose scent the Qur’án says his father caught from far away: I am conscious of the breath of Joseph.

It is “transformed by the winds and wafteth from the direction of the Ridván.” The Song of Solomon: awake, O north wind, and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out.
The Báb recalls being reared with compassion and then acquainted with God’s Revelation. The psalmist’s account of his life has the same shape: O God, thou hast taught me from my youth.
Pearls concealed in the shell and jewels “treasured in the seas of words.” The merchant of the parable sells all that he has for one pearl of great price.
“There upon the mountain, all alone, pray.” Jesus sent the multitudes away and went up into a mountain apart to pray; and when the evening was come, he was there alone.
Ecstasy is found alone on the mountain. Hillel’s rule in the Mishnah pulls the other way: do not separate yourself from the community. How do the guide’s own last readings answer him?
“I have journeyed through the unseen worlds and invisible realms.” Paul speaks of a man caught up to the third heaven, whether in the body or out of the body he cannot tell.
“The life-giving breeze is wafting.” Ezekiel in the valley of bones: come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.

diogenes-looking-for-a-man.text: He lit a lamp in broad daylight and said, as he went about, "I am looking for a man
diogenes-looking-for-a-man.author: Diogenes of Sinope, as reported by Diogenes Laërtius
diogenes-looking-for-a-man.year: 3rd century CE, of a saying of the 4th century BCE

herbert-love-bade-me-welcome.text: Love bade me welcome: yet my soul drew back, / Guiltie of dust and sinne. / But quick-ey'd Love, observing me grow slack / From my first entrance in, / Drew nearer to me, sweetly questioning, / If I lack'd any thing … You must sit down, sayes Love, and taste my meat: / So I did sit and eat
herbert-love-bade-me-welcome.author: George Herbert
herbert-love-bade-me-welcome.caveat: The spelling is that of the first edition.

shakespeare-lunatic-lover-poet.text: Lovers and madmen have such seething brains, / Such shaping fantasies, that apprehend / More than cool reason ever comprehends. / The lunatic, the lover and the poet / Are of imagination all compact
shakespeare-lunatic-lover-poet.author: William Shakespeare

song-fair-as-the-moon.text: Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners

song-awake-o-north-wind.text: Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits

song-sick-of-love.text: Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love

psalm-deep-calleth-unto-deep.text: Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me

revelation-worthy-to-open-the-book.text: And I saw a strong angel proclaiming with a loud voice, Who is worthy to open the book, and to loose the seals thereof? And no man in heaven, nor in earth, neither under the earth, was able to open the book, neither to look thereon. And I wept much, because no man was found worthy to open and to read the book, neither to look thereon. And one of the elders saith unto me, Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof

colossians-life-is-hid.text: For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God

matthew-up-into-a-mountain-apart.text: And when he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into a mountain apart to pray: and when the evening was come, he was there alone

corinthians-cup-of-blessing.text: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread
